chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Susukhaṁ vata jīvāma, yesaṁ no natthi kiñcanaṁ; Pītibhakkhā bhavissāma, devā ābhassarā yathā.
translation: Let us live happily then, though we call nothing our own! We shall be like the bright gods, feeding on happiness!

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Jayaṁ veraṁ pasavati, dukkhaṁ seti parājito; Upasanto sukhaṁ seti, hitvā jayaparājayaṁ.
translation: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Natthi rāgasamo aggi, Natthi dosasamo kali; Natthi khandhasamā dukkhā, Natthi santiparaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: There is no fire like passion; there is no losing throw like hatred; there is no pain like this body; there is no happiness higher than rest.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Jighacchāparamā rogā, saṅkhāraparamā dukhā; Etaṁ ñatvā yathābhūtaṁ, nibbānaṁ paramaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: Hunger is the worst of diseases, the body the greatest of pains; if one knows this truly, that is Nirvana, the highest happiness.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Ārogyaparamā lābhā, Santuṭṭhiparamaṁ dhanaṁ; Vissāsaparamā ñāti, Nibbānaṁ paramaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Pavivekarasaṁ pitvā, rasaṁ upasamassa ca; Niddaro hoti nippāpo, dhammapītirasaṁ pivaṁ.
translation: He who has tasted the sweetness of solitude and tranquillity, is free from fear and free from sin, while he tastes the sweetness of drinking in the law.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Sāhu dassanamariyānaṁ, sannivāso sadā sukho; Adassanena bālānaṁ, niccameva sukhī siyā.
translation: The sight of the elect (Arya) is good, to live with them is always happiness; if a man does not see fools, he will be truly happy.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Bālasaṅgatacārī hi, dīghamaddhāna socati; Dukkho bālehi saṁvāso, amitteneva sabbadā; Dhīro ca sukhasaṁvāso, ñātīnaṁva samāgamo.
translation: He who walks in the company of fools suffers a long way; company with fools, as with an enemy, is always painful; company with the wise is pleasure, like meeting with kinsfolk.

chapterSummary: Defines a durable happiness that has nothing to do with winning or possessing, only with letting go.
pali: Tasmā hi— Dhīrañca paññañca bahussutañca, Dhorayhasīlaṁ vatavantamariyaṁ; Taṁ tādisaṁ sappurisaṁ sumedhaṁ, Bhajetha nakkhattapathaṁva candimā.
translation: Therefore, one ought to follow the wise, the intelligent, the learned, the much enduring, the dutiful, the elect; one ought to follow a good and wise man, as the moon follows the path of the stars.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Ayoge yuñjamattānaṁ, yogasmiñca ayojayaṁ; Atthaṁ hitvā piyaggāhī, pihetattānuyoginaṁ.
translation: He who gives himself to vanity, and does not give himself to meditation, forgetting the real aim (of life) and grasping at pleasure, will in time envy him who has exerted himself in meditation.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Mā piyehi samāgañchi, appiyehi kudācanaṁ; Piyānaṁ adassanaṁ dukkhaṁ, appiyānañca dassanaṁ.
translation: Let no man ever look for what is pleasant, or what is unpleasant. Not to see what is pleasant is pain, and it is pain to see what is unpleasant.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Tasmā piyaṁ na kayirātha, piyāpāyo hi pāpako; Ganthā tesaṁ na vijjanti, yesaṁ natthi piyāppiyaṁ.
translation: Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil. Those who love nothing and hate nothing, have no fetters.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Piyato jāyatī soko, piyato jāyatī bhayaṁ; Piyato vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṁ.
translation: From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Pemato jāyatī soko, pemato jāyatī bhayaṁ; Pemato vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṁ.
translation: From affection comes grief, from affection comes fear; he who is free from affection knows neither grief nor fear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Ratiyā jāyatī soko, ratiyā jāyatī bhayaṁ; Ratiyā vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṁ.
translation: From lust comes grief, from lust comes fear; he who is free from lust knows neither grief nor fear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Kāmato jāyatī soko, kāmato jāyatī bhayaṁ; Kāmato vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṁ.
translation: From love comes grief, from love comes fear; he who is free from love knows neither grief nor fear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Taṇhāya jāyatī soko, taṇhāya jāyatī bhayaṁ; Taṇhāya vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṁ.
translation: From greed comes grief, from greed comes fear; he who is free from greed knows neither grief nor fear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Sīladassanasampannaṁ, dhammaṭṭhaṁ saccavedinaṁ; Attano kamma kubbānaṁ, taṁ jano kurute piyaṁ.
translation: He who possesses virtue and intelligence, who is just, speaks the truth, and does what is his own business, him the world will hold dear.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Chandajāto anakkhāte, Manasā ca phuṭo siyā; Kāmesu ca appaṭibaddhacitto, Uddhaṁsototi vuccati.
translation: He in whom a desire for the Ineffable (Nirvana) has sprung up, who is satisfied in his mind, and whose thoughts are not bewildered by love, he is called urdhvamsrotas (carried upwards by the stream).

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Cirappavāsiṁ purisaṁ, dūrato sotthimāgataṁ; Ñātimittā suhajjā ca, abhinandanti āgataṁ.
translation: Kinsmen, friends, and lovers salute a man who has been long away, and returns safe from afar.

chapterSummary: Warns that affection and craving pull in opposite directions from peace, and binds people to new pain.
pali: Tatheva katapuññampi, asmā lokā paraṁ gataṁ; Puññāni paṭigaṇhanti, piyaṁ ñātīva āgataṁ.
translation: In like manner his good works receive him who has done good, and has gone from this world to the other;--as kinsmen receive a friend on his return.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Kodhaṁ jahe vippajaheyya mānaṁ, Saṁyojanaṁ sabbamatikkameyya; Taṁ nāmarūpasmimasajjamānaṁ, Akiñcanaṁ nānupatanti dukkhā.
translation: Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage! No sufferings befall the man who is not attached to name and form, and who calls nothing his own.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Yo ve uppatitaṁ kodhaṁ, rathaṁ bhantaṁva vāraye; Tamahaṁ sārathiṁ brūmi, rasmiggāho itaro jano.
translation: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Akkodhena jine kodhaṁ, asādhuṁ sādhunā jine; Jine kadariyaṁ dānena, saccenālikavādinaṁ.
translation: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Saccaṁ bhaṇe na kujjheyya, dajjā appampi yācito; Etehi tīhi ṭhānehi, gacche devāna santike.
translation: Speak the truth, do not yield to anger; give, if thou art asked for little; by these three steps thou wilt go near the gods.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Ahiṁsakā ye munayo, niccaṁ kāyena saṁvutā; Te yanti accutaṁ ṭhānaṁ, yattha gantvā na socare.
translation: The sages who injure nobody, and who always control their body, they will go to the unchangeable place (Nirvana), where, if they have gone, they will suffer no more.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Sadā jāgaramānānaṁ, ahorattānusikkhinaṁ; Nibbānaṁ adhimuttānaṁ, atthaṁ gacchanti āsavā.
translation: Those who are ever watchful, who study day and night, and who strive after Nirvana, their passions will come to an end.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Porāṇametaṁ atula, netaṁ ajjatanāmiva; Nindanti tuṇhimāsīnaṁ, nindanti bahubhāṇinaṁ; Mitabhāṇimpi nindanti, natthi loke anindito.
translation: This is an old saying, O Atula, this is not only of to-day: `They blame him who sits silent, they blame him who speaks much, they also blame him who says little; there is no one on earth who is not blamed.'

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Na cāhu na ca bhavissati, na cetarahi vijjati; Ekantaṁ nindito poso, ekantaṁ vā pasaṁsito.
translation: There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Yañce viññū pasaṁsanti, anuvicca suve suve; Acchiddavuttiṁ medhāviṁ, paññāsīlasamāhitaṁ.
translation: But he whom those who discriminate praise continually day after day, as without blemish, wise, rich in knowledge and virtue, who would dare to blame him, like a coin made of gold from the Gambu river? Even the gods praise him, he is praised even by Brahman.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Nikkhaṁ jambonadasseva, ko taṁ ninditumarahati; Devāpi naṁ pasaṁsanti, brahmunāpi pasaṁsito.
translation: But he whom those who discriminate praise continually day after day, as without blemish, wise, rich in knowledge and virtue, who would dare to blame him, like a coin made of gold from the Gambu river? Even the gods praise him, he is praised even by Brahman.

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Kāyappakopaṁ rakkheyya, kāyena saṁvuto siyā; Kāyaduccaritaṁ hitvā, kāyena sucaritaṁ care.
translation: Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body! Leave the sins of the body, and with thy body practise virtue!

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Vacīpakopaṁ rakkheyya, vācāya saṁvuto siyā; Vacīduccaritaṁ hitvā, vācāya sucaritaṁ care.
translation: Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue! Leave the sins of the tongue, and practise virtue with thy tongue!

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Manopakopaṁ rakkheyya, manasā saṁvuto siyā; Manoduccaritaṁ hitvā, manasā sucaritaṁ care.
translation: Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind! Leave the sins of the mind, and practise virtue with thy mind!

chapterSummary: Treats anger as poison, arguing that patience is strength rather than passivity.
pali: Kāyena saṁvutā dhīrā, atho vācāya saṁvutā; Manasā saṁvutā dhīrā, te ve suparisaṁvutā.
translation: The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Paṇḍupalāsova dānisi, Yamapurisāpi ca te upaṭṭhitā; Uyyogamukhe ca tiṭṭhasi, Pātheyyampi ca te na vijjati.
translation: Thou art now like a sear leaf, the messengers of death (Yama) have come near to thee; thou standest at the door of thy departure, and thou hast no provision for thy journey.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: So karohi dīpamattano, Khippaṁ vāyama paṇḍito bhava; Niddhantamalo anaṅgaṇo, Dibbaṁ ariyabhūmiṁ upehisi.
translation: Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise! When thy impurities are blown away, and thou art free from guilt, thou wilt enter into the heavenly world of the elect (Ariya).

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Upanītavayo ca dānisi, Sampayātosi yamassa santikaṁ; Vāso te natthi antarā, Pātheyyampi ca te na vijjati.
translation: Thy life has come to an end, thou art come near to death (Yama), there is no resting-place for thee on the road, and thou hast no provision for thy journey.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: So karohi dīpamattano, Khippaṁ vāyama paṇḍito bhava; Niddhantamalo anaṅgaṇo, Na punaṁ jātijaraṁ upehisi.
translation: Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise! When thy impurities are blown away, and thou art free from guilt, thou wilt not enter again into birth and decay.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Anupubbena medhāvī, thokaṁ thokaṁ khaṇe khaṇe; Kammāro rajatasseva, niddhame malamattano.
translation: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Ayasāva malaṁ samuṭṭhitaṁ, Tatuṭṭhāya tameva khādati; Evaṁ atidhonacārinaṁ, Sāni kammāni nayanti duggatiṁ.
translation: As the impurity which springs from the iron, when it springs from it, destroys it; thus do a transgressor's own works lead him to the evil path.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Asajjhāyamalā mantā, anuṭṭhānamalā gharā; Malaṁ vaṇṇassa kosajjaṁ, pamādo rakkhato malaṁ.
translation: The taint of prayers is non-repetition; the taint of houses, non-repair; the taint of the body is sloth; the taint of a watchman, thoughtlessness.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Malitthiyā duccaritaṁ, maccheraṁ dadato malaṁ; Malā ve pāpakā dhammā, asmiṁ loke paramhi ca.
translation: Bad conduct is the taint of woman, greediness the taint of a benefactor; tainted are all evil ways in this world and in the next.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Tato malā malataraṁ, avijjā paramaṁ malaṁ; Etaṁ malaṁ pahantvāna, nimmalā hotha bhikkhavo.
translation: But there is a taint worse than all taints,--ignorance is the greatest taint. O mendicants! throw off that taint, and become taintless!

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Sujīvaṁ ahirikena, kākasūrena dhaṁsinā; Pakkhandinā pagabbhena, saṅkiliṭṭhena jīvitaṁ.
translation: Life is easy to live for a man who is without shame, a crow hero, a mischief-maker, an insulting, bold, and wretched fellow.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Hirīmatā ca dujjīvaṁ, niccaṁ sucigavesinā; Alīnenāppagabbhena, suddhājīvena passatā.
translation: But life is hard to live for a modest man, who always looks for what is pure, who is disinterested, quiet, spotless, and intelligent.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Yo pāṇamatipāteti, musāvādañca bhāsati; Loke adinnamādiyati, paradārañca gacchati.
translation: He who destroys life, who speaks untruth, who in this world takes what is not given him, who goes to another man's wife;

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Surāmerayapānañca, yo naro anuyuñjati; Idheva meso lokasmiṁ, mūlaṁ khaṇati attano.
translation: And the man who gives himself to drinking intoxicating liquors, he, even in this world, digs up his own root.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Evaṁ bho purisa jānāhi, pāpadhammā asaññatā; Mā taṁ lobho adhammo ca, ciraṁ dukkhāya randhayuṁ.
translation: O man, know this, that the unrestrained are in a bad state; take care that greediness and vice do not bring thee to grief for a long time!

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Dadāti ve yathāsaddhaṁ, yathāpasādanaṁ jano; Tattha yo ca maṅku bhavati, paresaṁ pānabhojane; Na so divā vā rattiṁ vā, samādhimadhigacchati.
translation: The world gives according to their faith or according to their pleasure: if a man frets about the food and the drink given to others, he will find no rest either by day or by night.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Yassa cetaṁ samucchinnaṁ, mūlaghaccaṁ samūhataṁ; Sa ve divā vā rattiṁ vā, samādhimadhigacchati.
translation: He in whom that feeling is destroyed, and taken out with the very root, finds rest by day and by night.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Natthi rāgasamo aggi, natthi dosasamo gaho; Natthi mohasamaṁ jālaṁ, natthi taṇhāsamā nadī.
translation: There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Sudassaṁ vajjamaññesaṁ, attano pana duddasaṁ; Paresaṁ hi so vajjāni, opunāti yathā bhusaṁ; Attano pana chādeti, kaliṁva kitavā saṭho.
translation: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṁ ujjhānasaññino; Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā.
translation: If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow, and he is far from the destruction of passions.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Ākāseva padaṁ natthi, samaṇo natthi bāhire; Papañcābhiratā pajā, nippapañcā tathāgatā.
translation: There is no path through the air, a man is not a Samana by outward acts. The world delights in vanity, the Tathagatas (the Buddhas) are free from vanity.

chapterSummary: Catalogs the small corruptions -- laziness, pride, envy -- that quietly erode a clear mind.
pali: Ākāseva padaṁ natthi, samaṇo natthi bāhire; Saṅkhārā sassatā natthi, natthi buddhānamiñjitaṁ.
translation: There is no path through the air, a man is not a Samana by outward acts. No creatures are eternal; but the awakened (Buddha) are never shaken.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tena hoti dhammaṭṭho, yenatthaṁ sāhasā naye; Yo ca atthaṁ anatthañca, ubho niccheyya paṇḍito.
translation: A man is not just if he carries a matter by violence; no, he who distinguishes both right and wrong, who is learned and leads others, not by violence, but by law and equity, and who is guarded by the law and intelligent, he is called just.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Asāhasena dhammena, samena nayatī pare; Dhammassa gutto medhāvī, “dhammaṭṭho”ti pavuccati.
translation: A man is not just if he carries a matter by violence; no, he who distinguishes both right and wrong, who is learned and leads others, not by violence, but by law and equity, and who is guarded by the law and intelligent, he is called just.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tena paṇḍito hoti, yāvatā bahu bhāsati; Khemī averī abhayo, “paṇḍito”ti pavuccati.
translation: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tāvatā dhammadharo, yāvatā bahu bhāsati; Yo ca appampi sutvāna, dhammaṁ kāyena passati; Sa ve dhammadharo hoti, yo dhammaṁ nappamajjati.
translation: A man is not a supporter of the law because he talks much; even if a man has learnt little, but sees the law bodily, he is a supporter of the law, a man who never neglects the law.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tena thero so hoti, yenassa palitaṁ siro; Paripakko vayo tassa, “moghajiṇṇo”ti vuccati.
translation: A man is not an elder because his head is grey; his age may be ripe, but he is called `Old-in-vain.'

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Yamhi saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṁsā saṁyamo damo; Sa ve vantamalo dhīro, “thero” iti pavuccati.
translation: He in whom there is truth, virtue, love, restraint, moderation, he who is free from impurity and is wise, he is called an elder.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na vākkaraṇamattena, vaṇṇapokkharatāya vā; Sādhurūpo naro hoti, issukī maccharī saṭho.
translation: An envious greedy, dishonest man does not become respectable by means of much talking only, or by the beauty of his complexion.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Yassa cetaṁ samucchinnaṁ, mūlaghaccaṁ samūhataṁ; Sa vantadoso medhāvī, “sādhurūpo”ti vuccati.
translation: He in whom all this is destroyed, and taken out with the very root, he, when freed from hatred and wise, is called respectable.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na muṇḍakena samaṇo, abbato alikaṁ bhaṇaṁ; Icchālobhasamāpanno, samaṇo kiṁ bhavissati.
translation: Not by tonsure does an undisciplined man who speaks falsehood become a Samana; can a man be a Samana who is still held captive by desire and greediness?

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Yo ca sameti pāpāni, aṇuṁthūlāni sabbaso; Samitattā hi pāpānaṁ, “samaṇo”ti pavuccati.
translation: He who always quiets the evil, whether small or large, he is called a Samana (a quiet man), because he has quieted all evil.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tena bhikkhu so hoti, yāvatā bhikkhate pare; Vissaṁ dhammaṁ samādāya, bhikkhu hoti na tāvatā.
translation: A man is not a mendicant (Bhikshu) simply because he asks others for alms; he who adopts the whole law is a Bhikshu, not he who only begs.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Yodha puññañca pāpañca, bāhetvā brahmacariyavā; Saṅkhāya loke carati, sa ve “bhikkhū”ti vuccati.
translation: He who is above good and evil, who is chaste, who with knowledge passes through the world, he indeed is called a Bhikshu.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na monena munī hoti, mūḷharūpo aviddasu; Yo ca tulaṁva paggayha, varamādāya paṇḍito.
translation: A man is not a Muni because he observes silence (mona, i.e. mauna), if he is foolish and ignorant; but the wise who, taking the balance, chooses the good and avoids evil, he is a Muni, and is a Muni thereby; he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Pāpāni parivajjeti, sa munī tena so muni; Yo munāti ubho loke, “muni” tena pavuccati.
translation: A man is not a Muni because he observes silence (mona, i.e. mauna), if he is foolish and ignorant; but the wise who, taking the balance, chooses the good and avoids evil, he is a Muni, and is a Muni thereby; he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na tena ariyo hoti, yena pāṇāni hiṁsati; Ahiṁsā sabbapāṇānaṁ, “ariyo”ti pavuccati.
translation: A man is not an elect (Ariya) because he injures living creatures; because he has pity on all living creatures, therefore is a man called Ariya.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Na sīlabbatamattena, bāhusaccena vā pana; Atha vā samādhilābhena, vivittasayanena vā.
translation: Not only by discipline and vows, not only by much learning, not by entering into a trance, not by sleeping alone, do I earn the happiness of release which no worldling can know. Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires.

chapterSummary: Describes the fair and settled person as someone whose judgment does not bend with convenience.
pali: Phusāmi nekkhammasukhaṁ, aputhujjanasevitaṁ; Bhikkhu vissāsamāpādi, appatto āsavakkhayaṁ.
translation: Not only by discipline and vows, not only by much learning, not by entering into a trance, not by sleeping alone, do I earn the happiness of release which no worldling can know. Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho, saccānaṁ caturo padā; Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṁ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā.
translation: The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Eseva maggo natthañño, Dassanassa visuddhiyā; Etañhi tumhe paṭipajjatha, Mārassetaṁ pamohanaṁ.
translation: This is the way, there is no other that leads to the purifying of intelligence. Go on this way! Everything else is the deceit of Mara (the tempter).

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Etañhi tumhe paṭipannā, dukkhassantaṁ karissatha; Akkhāto vo mayā maggo, aññāya sallakantanaṁ.
translation: If you go on this way, you will make an end of pain! The way was preached by me, when I had understood the removal of the thorns (in the flesh).

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Tumhehi kiccamātappaṁ, akkhātāro tathāgatā; Paṭipannā pamokkhanti, jhāyino mārabandhanā.
translation: You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti, yadā paññāya passati; Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.
translation: `All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: “Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā”ti, yadā paññāya passati; Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.
translation: `All created things are grief and pain,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: “Sabbe dhammā anattā”ti, yadā paññāya passati; Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.
translation: `All forms are unreal,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Uṭṭhānakālamhi anuṭṭhahāno, Yuvā balī ālasiyaṁ upeto; Saṁsannasaṅkappamano kusīto, Paññāya maggaṁ alaso na vindati.
translation: He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise, who, though young and strong, is full of sloth, whose will and thought are weak, that lazy and idle man will never find the way to knowledge.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Vācānurakkhī manasā susaṁvuto, Kāyena ca nākusalaṁ kayirā; Ete tayo kammapathe visodhaye, Ārādhaye maggamisippaveditaṁ.
translation: Watching his speech, well restrained in mind, let a man never commit any wrong with his body! Let a man but keep these three roads of action clear, and he will achieve the way which is taught by the wise.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Yogā ve jāyatī bhūri, ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo; Etaṁ dvedhāpathaṁ ñatvā, bhavāya vibhavāya ca; Tathāttānaṁ niveseyya, yathā bhūri pavaḍḍhati.
translation: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Vanaṁ chindatha mā rukkhaṁ, vanato jāyate bhayaṁ; Chetvā vanañca vanathañca, nibbanā hotha bhikkhavo.
translation: Cut down the whole forest (of lust), not a tree only! Danger comes out of the forest (of lust). When you have cut down both the forest (of lust) and its undergrowth, then, Bhikshus, you will be rid of the forest and free!

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Yāva hi vanatho na chijjati, Aṇumattopi narassa nārisu; Paṭibaddhamanova tāva so, Vaccho khīrapakova mātari.
translation: So long as the love of man towards women, even the smallest, is not destroyed, so long is his mind in bondage, as the calf that drinks milk is to its mother.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Ucchinda sinehamattano, Kumudaṁ sāradikaṁva pāṇinā; Santimaggameva brūhaya, Nibbānaṁ sugatena desitaṁ.
translation: Cut out the love of self, like an autumn lotus, with thy hand! Cherish the road of peace. Nirvana has been shown by Sugata (Buddha).

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Idha vassaṁ vasissāmi, idha hemantagimhisu; Iti bālo vicinteti, antarāyaṁ na bujjhati.
translation: `Here I shall dwell in the rain, here in winter and summer,' thus the fool meditates, and does not think of his death.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Taṁ puttapasusammattaṁ, byāsattamanasaṁ naraṁ; Suttaṁ gāmaṁ mahoghova, maccu ādāya gacchati.
translation: Death comes and carries off that man, praised for his children and flocks, his mind distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Na santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā nāpi bandhavā; Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā.
translation: Sons are no help, nor a father, nor relations; there is no help from kinsfolk for one whom death has seized.

chapterSummary: Lays out the eightfold path itself as the one road that actually leads where it claims to.
pali: Etamatthavasaṁ ñatvā, paṇḍito sīlasaṁvuto; Nibbānagamanaṁ maggaṁ, khippameva visodhaye.
translation: A wise and good man who knows the meaning of this, should quickly clear the way that leads to Nirvana.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Mattāsukhapariccāgā, passe ce vipulaṁ sukhaṁ; Caje mattāsukhaṁ dhīro, sampassaṁ vipulaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Paradukkhūpadhānena, attano sukhamicchati; Verasaṁsaggasaṁsaṭṭho, verā so na parimuccati.
translation: He who, by causing pain to others, wishes to obtain pleasure for himself, he, entangled in the bonds of hatred, will never be free from hatred.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Yañhi kiccaṁ apaviddhaṁ, akiccaṁ pana karīyati; Unnaḷānaṁ pamattānaṁ, tesaṁ vaḍḍhanti āsavā.
translation: What ought to be done is neglected, what ought not to be done is done; the desires of unruly, thoughtless people are always increasing.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Yesañca susamāraddhā, niccaṁ kāyagatā sati; Akiccaṁ te na sevanti, kicce sātaccakārino; Satānaṁ sampajānānaṁ, atthaṁ gacchanti āsavā.
translation: But they whose whole watchfulness is always directed to their body, who do not follow what ought not to be done, and who steadfastly do what ought to be done, the desires of such watchful and wise people will come to an end.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Mātaraṁ pitaraṁ hantvā, rājāno dve ca khattiye; Raṭṭhaṁ sānucaraṁ hantvā, anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo.
translation: A true Brahmana goes scatheless, though he have killed father and mother, and two valiant kings, though he has destroyed a kingdom with all its subjects.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Mātaraṁ pitaraṁ hantvā, rājāno dve ca sotthiye; Veyagghapañcamaṁ hantvā, anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo.
translation: A true Brahmana goes scatheless, though he have killed father and mother, and two holy kings, and an eminent man besides.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, niccaṁ buddhagatā sati.
translation: The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, niccaṁ dhammagatā sati.
translation: The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on the law.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, niccaṁ saṅghagatā sati.
translation: The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on the church.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, niccaṁ kāyagatā sati.
translation: The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on their body.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, ahiṁsāya rato mano.
translation: The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their mind day and night always delights in compassion.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Suppabuddhaṁ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā; Yesaṁ divā ca ratto ca, bhāvanāya rato mano.
translation: The disciples of Gotama are always well awake, and their mind day and night always delights in meditation.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Duppabbajjaṁ durabhiramaṁ, Durāvāsā gharā dukhā; Dukkhosamānasaṁvāso, Dukkhānupatitaddhagū; Tasmā na caddhagū siyā, Na ca dukkhānupatito siyā.
translation: It is hard to leave the world (to become a friar), it is hard to enjoy the world; hard is the monastery, painful are the houses; painful it is to dwell with equals (to share everything in common) and the itinerant mendicant is beset with pain. Therefore let no man be an itinerant mendicant and he will not be beset with pain.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Saddho sīlena sampanno, yasobhogasamappito; Yaṁ yaṁ padesaṁ bhajati, tattha tattheva pūjito.
translation: Whatever place a faithful, virtuous, celebrated, and wealthy man chooses, there he is respected.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Dūre santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato; Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṁ khittā yathā sarā.
translation: Good people shine from afar, like the snowy mountains; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night.

chapterSummary: Gathers a mix of practical observations that did not fit neatly into any single chapter.
pali: Ekāsanaṁ ekaseyyaṁ, eko caramatandito; Eko damayamattānaṁ, vanante ramito siyā.
translation: He alone who, without ceasing, practises the duty of sitting alone and sleeping alone, he, subduing himself, will rejoice in the destruction of all desires alone, as if living in a forest.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Abhūtavādī nirayaṁ upeti, Yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha; Ubhopi te pecca samā bhavanti, Nihīnakammā manujā parattha.
translation: He who says what is not, goes to hell; he also who, having done a thing, says I have not done it. After death both are equal, they are men with evil deeds in the next world.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Kāsāvakaṇṭhā bahavo, pāpadhammā asaññatā; Pāpā pāpehi kammehi, nirayaṁ te upapajjare.
translation: Many men whose shoulders are covered with the yellow gown are ill-conditioned and unrestrained; such evil-doers by their evil deeds go to hell.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Seyyo ayoguḷo bhutto, tatto aggisikhūpamo; Yañce bhuñjeyya dussīlo, raṭṭhapiṇḍamasaññato.
translation: Better it would be to swallow a heated iron ball, like flaring fire, than that a bad unrestrained fellow should live on the charity of the land.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Cattāri ṭhānāni naro pamatto, Āpajjati paradārūpasevī; Apuññalābhaṁ na nikāmaseyyaṁ, Nindaṁ tatīyaṁ nirayaṁ catutthaṁ.
translation: Four things does a wreckless man gain who covets his neighbour's wife,--a bad reputation, an uncomfortable bed, thirdly, punishment, and lastly, hell.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Apuññalābho ca gatī ca pāpikā, Bhītassa bhītāya ratī ca thokikā; Rājā ca daṇḍaṁ garukaṁ paṇeti, Tasmā naro paradāraṁ na seve.
translation: There is bad reputation, and the evil way (to hell), there is the short pleasure of the frightened in the arms of the frightened, and the king imposes heavy punishment; therefore let no man think of his neighbour's wife.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Kuso yathā duggahito, hatthamevānukantati; Sāmaññaṁ dupparāmaṭṭhaṁ, nirayāyupakaḍḍhati.
translation: As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Yaṁ kiñci sithilaṁ kammaṁ, saṅkiliṭṭhañca yaṁ vataṁ; Saṅkassaraṁ brahmacariyaṁ, na taṁ hoti mahapphalaṁ.
translation: An act carelessly performed, a broken vow, and hesitating obedience to discipline, all this brings no great reward.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Kayirā ce kayirāthenaṁ, daḷhamenaṁ parakkame; Sithilo hi paribbājo, bhiyyo ākirate rajaṁ.
translation: If anything is to be done, let a man do it, let him attack it vigorously! A careless pilgrim only scatters the dust of his passions more widely.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Akataṁ dukkaṭaṁ seyyo, pacchā tappati dukkaṭaṁ; Katañca sukataṁ seyyo, yaṁ katvā nānutappati.
translation: An evil deed is better left undone, for a man repents of it afterwards; a good deed is better done, for having done it, one does not repent.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Nagaraṁ yathā paccantaṁ, guttaṁ santarabāhiraṁ; Evaṁ gopetha attānaṁ, khaṇo vo mā upaccagā; Khaṇātītā hi socanti, nirayamhi samappitā.
translation: Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself. Not a moment should escape, for they who allow the right moment to pass, suffer pain when they are in hell.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Alajjitāye lajjanti, lajjitāye na lajjare; Micchādiṭṭhisamādānā, sattā gacchanti duggatiṁ.
translation: They who are ashamed of what they ought not to be ashamed of, and are not ashamed of what they ought to be ashamed of, such men, embracing false doctrines enter the evil path.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Abhaye bhayadassino, bhaye cābhayadassino; Micchādiṭṭhisamādānā, sattā gacchanti duggatiṁ.
translation: They who fear when they ought not to fear, and fear not when they ought to fear, such men, embracing false doctrines, enter the evil path.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Avajje vajjamatino, vajje cāvajjadassino; Micchādiṭṭhisamādānā, sattā gacchanti duggatiṁ.
translation: They who forbid when there is nothing to be forbidden, and forbid not when there is something to be forbidden, such men, embracing false doctrines, enter the evil path.

chapterSummary: Looks unflinchingly at the consequences of a wasted or harmful life.
pali: Vajjañca vajjato ñatvā, avajjañca avajjato; Sammādiṭṭhisamādānā, sattā gacchanti suggatiṁ.
translation: They who know what is forbidden as forbidden, and what is not forbidden as not forbidden, such men, embracing the true doctrine, enter the good path.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Ahaṁ nāgova saṅgāme, cāpato patitaṁ saraṁ; Ativākyaṁ titikkhissaṁ, dussīlo hi bahujjano.
translation: Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Dantaṁ nayanti samitiṁ, dantaṁ rājābhirūhati; Danto seṭṭho manussesu, yotivākyaṁ titikkhati.
translation: They lead a tamed elephant to battle, the king mounts a tamed elephant; the tamed is the best among men, he who silently endures abuse.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Varamassatarā dantā, ājānīyā ca sindhavā; Kuñjarā ca mahānāgā, attadanto tato varaṁ.
translation: Mules are good, if tamed, and noble Sindhu horses, and elephants with large tusks; but he who tames himself is better still.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Na hi etehi yānehi, gaccheyya agataṁ disaṁ; Yathāttanā sudantena, danto dantena gacchati.
translation: For with these animals does no man reach the untrodden country (Nirvana), where a tamed man goes on a tamed animal, viz. on his own well-tamed self.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Dhanapālo nāma kuñjaro, Kaṭukabhedano dunnivārayo; Baddho kabaḷaṁ na bhuñjati, Sumarati nāgavanassa kuñjaro.
translation: The elephant called Dhanapalaka, his temples running with sap, and difficult to hold, does not eat a morsel when bound; the elephant longs for the elephant grove.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Middhī yadā hoti mahagghaso ca, Niddāyitā samparivattasāyī; Mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho, Punappunaṁ gabbhamupeti mando.
translation: If a man becomes fat and a great eater, if he is sleepy and rolls himself about, that fool, like a hog fed on wash, is born again and again.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Idaṁ pure cittamacāri cārikaṁ, Yenicchakaṁ yatthakāmaṁ yathāsukhaṁ; Tadajjahaṁ niggahessāmi yoniso, Hatthippabhinnaṁ viya aṅkusaggaho.
translation: This mind of mine went formerly wandering about as it liked, as it listed, as it pleased; but I shall now hold it in thoroughly, as the rider who holds the hook holds in the furious elephant.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Appamādaratā hotha, sacittamanurakkhatha; Duggā uddharathattānaṁ, paṅke sannova kuñjaro.
translation: Be not thoughtless, watch your thoughts! Draw yourself out of the evil way, like an elephant sunk in mud.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Sace labhetha nipakaṁ sahāyaṁ, Saddhiṁ caraṁ sādhuvihāridhīraṁ; Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni, Careyya tenattamano satīmā.
translation: If a man find a prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, he may walk with him, overcoming all dangers, happy, but considerate.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: No ce labhetha nipakaṁ sahāyaṁ, Saddhiṁ caraṁ sādhuvihāridhīraṁ; Rājāva raṭṭhaṁ vijitaṁ pahāya, Eko care mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo.
translation: If a man find no prudent companion who walks with him, is wise, and lives soberly, let him walk alone, like a king who has left his conquered country behind,--like an elephant in the forest.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Ekassa caritaṁ seyyo, Natthi bāle sahāyatā; Eko care na ca pāpāni kayirā, Appossukko mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo.
translation: It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Atthamhi jātamhi sukhā sahāyā, Tuṭṭhī sukhā yā itarītarena; Puññaṁ sukhaṁ jīvitasaṅkhayamhi, Sabbassa dukkhassa sukhaṁ pahānaṁ.
translation: If an occasion arises, friends are pleasant; enjoyment is pleasant, whatever be the cause; a good work is pleasant in the hour of death; the giving up of all grief is pleasant.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Sukhā matteyyatā loke, atho petteyyatā sukhā; Sukhā sāmaññatā loke, atho brahmaññatā sukhā.
translation: Pleasant in the world is the state of a mother, pleasant the state of a father, pleasant the state of a Samana, pleasant the state of a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Uses the trained elephant as a long metaphor for a mind brought under control through patience.
pali: Sukhaṁ yāva jarā sīlaṁ, sukhā saddhā patiṭṭhitā; Sukho paññāya paṭilābho, pāpānaṁ akaraṇaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: Pleasant is virtue lasting to old age, pleasant is a faith firmly rooted; pleasant is attainment of intelligence, pleasant is avoiding of sins.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Manujassa pamattacārino, Taṇhā vaḍḍhati māluvā viya; So plavatī hurā huraṁ, Phalamicchaṁva vanasmi vānaro.
translation: The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Yaṁ esā sahate jammī, taṇhā loke visattikā; Sokā tassa pavaḍḍhanti, abhivaṭṭhaṁva bīraṇaṁ.
translation: Whomsoever this fierce thirst overcomes, full of poison, in this world, his sufferings increase like the abounding Birana grass.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Yo cetaṁ sahate jammiṁ, taṇhaṁ loke duraccayaṁ; Sokā tamhā papatanti, udabinduva pokkharā.
translation: He who overcomes this fierce thirst, difficult to be conquered in this world, sufferings fall off from him, like water-drops from a lotus leaf.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Taṁ vo vadāmi bhaddaṁ vo, yāvantettha samāgatā; Taṇhāya mūlaṁ khaṇatha, usīratthova bīraṇaṁ; Mā vo naḷaṁva sotova, māro bhañji punappunaṁ.
translation: This salutary word I tell you, `Do ye, as many as are here assembled, dig up the root of thirst, as he who wants the sweet-scented Usira root must dig up the Birana grass, that Mara (the tempter) may not crush you again and again, as the stream crushes the reeds.'

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe, Chinnopi rukkho punareva rūhati; Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate, Nibbattatī dukkhamidaṁ punappunaṁ.
translation: As a tree, even though it has been cut down, is firm so long as its root is safe, and grows again, thus, unless the feeders of thirst are destroyed, the pain (of life) will return again and again.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Yassa chattiṁsati sotā, manāpasavanā bhusā; Mahāvahanti duddiṭṭhiṁ, saṅkappā rāganissitā.
translation: He whose thirst running towards pleasure is exceeding strong in the thirty-six channels, the waves will carry away that misguided man, viz. his desires which are set on passion.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Savanti sabbadhi sotā, latā uppajja tiṭṭhati; Tañca disvā lataṁ jātaṁ, mūlaṁ paññāya chindatha.
translation: The channels run everywhere, the creeper (of passion) stands sprouting; if you see the creeper springing up, cut its root by means of knowledge.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Saritāni sinehitāni ca, Somanassāni bhavanti jantuno; Te sātasitā sukhesino, Te ve jātijarūpagā narā.
translation: A creature's pleasures are extravagant and luxurious; sunk in lust and looking for pleasure, men undergo (again and again) birth and decay.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tasiṇāya purakkhatā pajā, Parisappanti sasova bandhito; Saṁyojanasaṅgasattakā, Dukkhamupenti punappunaṁ cirāya.
translation: Men, driven on by thirst, run about like a snared hare; held in fetters and bonds, they undergo pain for a long time, again and again.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tasiṇāya purakkhatā pajā, Parisappanti sasova bandhito; Tasmā tasiṇaṁ vinodaye, Ākaṅkhanta virāgamattano.
translation: Men, driven on by thirst, run about like a snared hare; let therefore the mendicant drive out thirst, by striving after passionlessness for himself.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Yo nibbanatho vanādhimutto, Vanamutto vanameva dhāvati; Taṁ puggalametha passatha, Mutto bandhanameva dhāvati.
translation: He who having got rid of the forest (of lust) (i.e. after having reached Nirvana) gives himself over to forest-life (i.e. to lust), and who, when removed from the forest (i.e. from lust), runs to the forest (i.e. to lust), look at that man! though free, he runs into bondage.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Na taṁ daḷhaṁ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, Yadāyasaṁ dārujapabbajañca; Sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu, Puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā.
translation: Wise people do not call that a strong fetter which is made of iron, wood, or hemp; far stronger is the care for precious stones and rings, for sons and a wife.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Etaṁ daḷhaṁ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, Ohārinaṁ sithilaṁ duppamuñcaṁ; Etampi chetvāna paribbajanti, Anapekkhino kāmasukhaṁ pahāya.
translation: That fetter wise people call strong which drags down, yields, but is difficult to undo; after having cut this at last, people leave the world, free from cares, and leaving desires and pleasures behind.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Ye rāgarattānupatanti sotaṁ, Sayaṅkataṁ makkaṭakova jālaṁ; Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā, Anapekkhino sabbadukkhaṁ pahāya.
translation: Those who are slaves to passions, run down with the stream (of desires), as a spider runs down the web which he has made himself; when they have cut this, at last, wise people leave the world free from cares, leaving all affection behind.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Muñca pure muñca pacchato, Majjhe muñca bhavassa pāragū; Sabbattha vimuttamānaso, Na punaṁ jātijaraṁ upehisi.
translation: Give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle, when thou goest to the other shore of existence; if thy mind is altogether free, thou wilt not again enter into birth and decay.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Vitakkamathitassa jantuno, Tibbarāgassa subhānupassino; Bhiyyo taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, Esa kho daḷhaṁ karoti bandhanaṁ.
translation: If a man is tossed about by doubts, full of strong passions, and yearning only for what is delightful, his thirst will grow more and more, and he will indeed make his fetters strong.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Vitakkūpasame ca yo rato, Asubhaṁ bhāvayate sadā sato; Esa kho byanti kāhiti, Esa checchati mārabandhanaṁ.
translation: If a man delights in quieting doubts, and, always reflecting, dwells on what is not delightful (the impurity of the body, &c.), he certainly will remove, nay, he will cut the fetter of Mara.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Niṭṭhaṅgato asantāsī, vītataṇho anaṅgaṇo; Acchindi bhavasallāni, antimoyaṁ samussayo.
translation: He who has reached the consummation, who does not tremble, who is without thirst and without sin, he has broken all the thorns of life: this will be his last body.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Vītataṇho anādāno, Niruttipadakovido; Akkharānaṁ sannipātaṁ, Jaññā pubbāparāni ca; Sa ve “antimasārīro, Mahāpañño mahāpuriso”ti vuccati.
translation: He who is without thirst and without affection, who understands the words and their interpretation, who knows the order of letters (those which are before and which are after), he has received his last body, he is called the great sage, the great man.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmi, Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto; Sabbañjaho taṇhakkhaye vimutto, Sayaṁ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṁ.
translation: `I have conquered all, I know all, in all conditions of life I am free from taint; I have left all, and through the destruction of thirst I am free; having learnt myself, whom shall I teach?'

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Sabbadānaṁ dhammadānaṁ jināti, Sabbarasaṁ dhammaraso jināti; Sabbaratiṁ dhammarati jināti, Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṁ jināti.
translation: The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Hananti bhogā dummedhaṁ, no ca pāragavesino; Bhogataṇhāya dummedho, hanti aññeva attanaṁ.
translation: Pleasures destroy the foolish, if they look not for the other shore; the foolish by his thirst for pleasures destroys himself, as if he were his own enemy.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tiṇadosāni khettāni, rāgadosā ayaṁ pajā; Tasmā hi vītarāgesu, dinnaṁ hoti mahapphalaṁ.
translation: The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by passion: therefore a gift bestowed on the passionless brings great reward.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tiṇadosāni khettāni, dosadosā ayaṁ pajā; Tasmā hi vītadosesu, dinnaṁ hoti mahapphalaṁ.
translation: The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by hatred: therefore a gift bestowed on those who do not hate brings great reward.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tiṇadosāni khettāni, mohadosā ayaṁ pajā; Tasmā hi vītamohesu, dinnaṁ hoti mahapphalaṁ.
translation: The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by vanity: therefore a gift bestowed on those who are free from vanity brings great reward.

chapterSummary: Names craving as the force that keeps rebuilding suffering, like a vine that grows back after cutting.
pali: Tiṇadosāni khettāni, icchādosā ayaṁ pajā; Tasmā hi vigaticchesu, dinnaṁ hoti mahapphalaṁ.
translation: The fields are damaged by weeds, mankind is damaged by lust: therefore a gift bestowed on those who are free from lust brings great reward.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Cakkhunā saṁvaro sādhu, sādhu sotena saṁvaro; Ghānena saṁvaro sādhu, sādhu jivhāya saṁvaro.
translation: Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear, in the nose restraint is good, good is restraint in the tongue.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Kāyena saṁvaro sādhu, sādhu vācāya saṁvaro; Manasā saṁvaro sādhu, sādhu sabbattha saṁvaro; Sabbattha saṁvuto bhikkhu, sabbadukkhā pamuccati.
translation: In the body restraint is good, good is restraint in speech, in thought restraint is good, good is restraint in all things. A Bhikshu, restrained in all things, is freed from all pain.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Hatthasaṁyato pādasaṁyato, Vācāsaṁyato saṁyatuttamo; Ajjhattarato samāhito, Eko santusito tamāhu bhikkhuṁ.
translation: He who controls his hand, he who controls his feet, he who controls his speech, he who is well controlled, he who delights inwardly, who is collected, who is solitary and content, him they call Bhikshu.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Yo mukhasaṁyato bhikkhu, mantabhāṇī anuddhato; Atthaṁ dhammañca dīpeti, madhuraṁ tassa bhāsitaṁ.
translation: The Bhikshu who controls his mouth, who speaks wisely and calmly, who teaches the meaning and the law, his word is sweet.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Dhammārāmo dhammarato, dhammaṁ anuvicintayaṁ; Dhammaṁ anussaraṁ bhikkhu, saddhammā na parihāyati.
translation: He who dwells in the law, delights in the law, meditates on the law, follows the law, that Bhikshu will never fall away from the true law.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Salābhaṁ nātimaññeyya, nāññesaṁ pihayaṁ care; Aññesaṁ pihayaṁ bhikkhu, samādhiṁ nādhigacchati.
translation: Let him not despise what he has received, nor ever envy others: a mendicant who envies others does not obtain peace of mind.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Appalābhopi ce bhikkhu, salābhaṁ nātimaññati; Taṁ ve devā pasaṁsanti, suddhājīviṁ atanditaṁ.
translation: A Bhikshu who, though he receives little, does not despise what he has received, even the gods will praise him, if his life is pure, and if he is not slothful.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Sabbaso nāmarūpasmiṁ, yassa natthi mamāyitaṁ; Asatā ca na socati, sa ve “bhikkhū”ti vuccati.
translation: He who never identifies himself with name and form, and does not grieve over what is no more, he indeed is called a Bhikshu.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Mettāvihārī yo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane; Adhigacche padaṁ santaṁ, saṅkhārūpasamaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: The Bhikshu who acts with kindness, who is calm in the doctrine of Buddha, will reach the quiet place (Nirvana), cessation of natural desires, and happiness.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Siñca bhikkhu imaṁ nāvaṁ, sittā te lahumessati; Chetvā rāgañca dosañca, tato nibbānamehisi.
translation: O Bhikshu, empty this boat! if emptied, it will go quickly; having cut off passion and hatred thou wilt go to Nirvana.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Pañca chinde pañca jahe, pañca cuttari bhāvaye; Pañca saṅgātigo bhikkhu, “oghatiṇṇo”ti vuccati.
translation: Cut off the five (senses), leave the five, rise above the five. A Bhikshu, who has escaped from the five fetters, he is called Oghatinna, `saved from the flood.'

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Jhāya bhikkhu mā pamādo, Mā te kāmaguṇe ramessu cittaṁ; Mā lohaguḷaṁ gilī pamatto, Mā kandi “dukkhamidan”ti dayhamāno.
translation: Meditate, O Bhikshu, and be not heedless! Do not direct thy thought to what gives pleasure that thou mayest not for thy heedlessness have to swallow the iron ball (in hell), and that thou mayest not cry out when burning, `This is pain.'

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Natthi jhānaṁ apaññassa, paññā natthi ajhāyato; Yamhi jhānañca paññā ca, sa ve nibbānasantike.
translation: Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Suññāgāraṁ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno; Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṁ vipassato.
translation: A Bhikshu who has entered his empty house, and whose mind is tranquil, feels a more than human delight when he sees the law clearly.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṁ udayabbayaṁ; Labhatī pītipāmojjaṁ, amataṁ taṁ vijānataṁ.
translation: As soon as he has considered the origin and destruction of the elements (khandha) of the body, he finds happiness and joy which belong to those who know the immortal (Nirvana).

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Tatrāyamādi bhavati, idha paññassa bhikkhuno; Indriyagutti santuṭṭhi, pātimokkhe ca saṁvaro.
translation: And this is the beginning here for a wise Bhikshu: watchfulness over the senses, contentedness, restraint under the law; keep noble friends whose life is pure, and who are not slothful.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Mitte bhajassu kalyāṇe, suddhājīve atandite; Paṭisanthāravutyassa, ācārakusalo siyā; Tato pāmojjabahulo, dukkhassantaṁ karissati.
translation: Let him live in charity, let him be perfect in his duties; then in the fulness of delight he will make an end of suffering.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Vassikā viya pupphāni, maddavāni pamuñcati; Evaṁ rāgañca dosañca, vippamuñcetha bhikkhavo.
translation: As the Vassika plant sheds its withered flowers, men should shed passion and hatred, O ye Bhikshus!

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Santakāyo santavāco, santavā susamāhito; Vantalokāmiso bhikkhu, “upasanto”ti vuccati.
translation: The Bhikshu whose body and tongue and mind are quieted, who is collected, and has rejected the baits of the world, he is called quiet.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Attanā codayattānaṁ, paṭimaṁsetha attanā; So attagutto satimā, sukhaṁ bhikkhu vihāhisi.
translation: Rouse thyself by thyself, examine thyself by thyself, thus self-protected and attentive wilt thou live happily, O Bhikshu!

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Attā hi attano nātho, ko hi nātho paro siyā; Attā hi attano gati, tasmā saṁyamamattānaṁ; Assaṁ bhadraṁva vāṇijo.
translation: For self is the lord of self, self is the refuge of self; therefore curb thyself as the merchant curbs a good horse.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane; Adhigacche padaṁ santaṁ, saṅkhārūpasamaṁ sukhaṁ.
translation: The Bhikshu, full of delight, who is calm in the doctrine of Buddha will reach the quiet place (Nirvana), cessation of natural desires, and happiness.

chapterSummary: Describes the discipline of the wandering monk, and what separates real practice from mere appearance.
pali: Yo have daharo bhikkhu, yuñjati buddhasāsane; Somaṁ lokaṁ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā.
translation: He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Chinda sotaṁ parakkamma, kāme panuda brāhmaṇa; Saṅkhārānaṁ khayaṁ ñatvā, akataññūsi brāhmaṇa.
translation: Stop the stream valiantly, drive away the desires, O Brahmana! When you have understood the destruction of all that was made, you will understand that which was not made.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yadā dvayesu dhammesu, pāragū hoti brāhmaṇo; Athassa sabbe saṁyogā, atthaṁ gacchanti jānato.
translation: If the Brahmana has reached the other shore in both laws (in restraint and contemplation), all bonds vanish from him who has obtained knowledge.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yassa pāraṁ apāraṁ vā, pārāpāraṁ na vijjati; Vītaddaraṁ visaṁyuttaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: He for whom there is neither this nor that shore, nor both, him, the fearless and unshackled, I call indeed a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Jhāyiṁ virajamāsīnaṁ, katakiccamanāsavaṁ; Uttamatthamanuppattaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: He who is thoughtful, blameless, settled, dutiful, without passions, and who has attained the highest end, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Divā tapati ādicco, rattimābhāti candimā; Sannaddho khattiyo tapati, jhāyī tapati brāhmaṇo; Atha sabbamahorattiṁ, buddho tapati tejasā.
translation: The sun is bright by day, the moon shines by night, the warrior is bright in his armour, the Brahmana is bright in his meditation; but Buddha, the Awakened, is bright with splendour day and night.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Bāhitapāpoti brāhmaṇo, Samacariyā samaṇoti vuccati; Pabbājayamattano malaṁ, Tasmā “pabbajito”ti vuccati.
translation: Because a man is rid of evil, therefore he is called Brahmana; because he walks quietly, therefore he is called Samana; because he has sent away his own impurities, therefore he is called Pravragita (Pabbagita, a pilgrim).

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Na brāhmaṇassa pahareyya, nāssa muñcetha brāhmaṇo; Dhī brāhmaṇassa hantāraṁ, tato dhī yassa muñcati.
translation: No one should attack a Brahmana, but no Brahmana (if attacked) should let himself fly at his aggressor! Woe to him who strikes a Brahmana, more woe to him who flies at his aggressor!

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Na brāhmaṇassetadakiñci seyyo, Yadā nisedho manaso piyehi; Yato yato hiṁsamano nivattati, Tato tato sammatimeva dukkhaṁ.
translation: It advantages a Brahmana not a little if he holds his mind back from the pleasures of life; when all wish to injure has vanished, pain will cease.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yassa kāyena vācāya, manasā natthi dukkaṭaṁ; Saṁvutaṁ tīhi ṭhānehi, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not offend by body, word, or thought, and is controlled on these three points.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yamhā dhammaṁ vijāneyya, sammāsambuddhadesitaṁ; Sakkaccaṁ taṁ namasseyya, aggihuttaṁva brāhmaṇo.
translation: After a man has once understood the law as taught by the Well-awakened (Buddha), let him worship it carefully, as the Brahmana worships the sacrificial fire.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Na jaṭāhi na gottena, na jaccā hoti brāhmaṇo; Yamhi saccañca dhammo ca, so sucī so ca brāhmaṇo.
translation: A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Kiṁ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṁ te ajinasāṭiyā; Abbhantaraṁ te gahanaṁ, bāhiraṁ parimajjasi.
translation: What is the use of platted hair, O fool! what of the raiment of goat-skins? Within thee there is ravening, but the outside thou makest clean.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Paṁsukūladharaṁ jantuṁ, kisaṁ dhamanisanthataṁ; Ekaṁ vanasmiṁ jhāyantaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: The man who wears dirty raiments, who is emaciated and covered with veins, who lives alone in the forest, and meditates, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Na cāhaṁ brāhmaṇaṁ brūmi, yonijaṁ mattisambhavaṁ; Bhovādi nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano; Akiñcanaṁ anādānaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: I do not call a man a Brahmana because of his origin or of his mother. He is indeed arrogant, and he is wealthy: but the poor, who is free from all attachments, him I call indeed a Brahmana.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Sabbasaṁyojanaṁ chetvā, yo ve na paritassati; Saṅgātigaṁ visaṁyuttaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has cut all fetters, who never trembles, is independent and unshackled.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Chetvā naddhiṁ varattañca, sandānaṁ sahanukkamaṁ; Ukkhittapalighaṁ buddhaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who has cut the strap and the thong, the chain with all that pertains to it, who has burst the bar, and is awakened.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Akkosaṁ vadhabandhañca, aduṭṭho yo titikkhati; Khantībalaṁ balānīkaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, though he has committed no offence, endures reproach, bonds, and stripes, who has endurance for his force, and strength for his army.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Akkodhanaṁ vatavantaṁ, sīlavantaṁ anussadaṁ; Dantaṁ antimasārīraṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who is free from anger, dutiful, virtuous, without appetite, who is subdued, and has received his last body.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Vāri pokkharapatteva, āraggeriva sāsapo; Yo na limpati kāmesu, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yo dukkhassa pajānāti, idheva khayamattano; Pannabhāraṁ visaṁyuttaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who, even here, knows the end of his suffering, has put down his burden, and is unshackled.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Gambhīrapaññaṁ medhāviṁ, maggāmaggassa kovidaṁ; Uttamatthamanuppattaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana whose knowledge is deep, who possesses wisdom, who knows the right way and the wrong, and has attained the highest end.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Asaṁsaṭṭhaṁ gahaṭṭhehi, anāgārehi cūbhayaṁ; Anokasārimappicchaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who keeps aloof both from laymen and from mendicants, who frequents no houses, and has but few desires.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Nidhāya daṇḍaṁ bhūtesu, tasesu thāvaresu ca; Yo na hanti na ghāteti, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who finds no fault with other beings, whether feeble or strong, and does not kill nor cause slaughter.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Aviruddhaṁ viruddhesu, attadaṇḍesu nibbutaṁ; Sādānesu anādānaṁ, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who is tolerant with the intolerant, mild with fault-finders, and free from passion among the passionate.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
pali: Yassa rāgo ca doso ca, māno makkho ca pātito; Sāsaporiva āraggā, tamahaṁ brūmi brāhmaṇaṁ.
translation: Him I call indeed a Brahmana from whom anger and hatred, pride and envy have dropt like a mustard seed from the point of a needle.

chapterSummary: Closes by redefining who deserves to be called noble: not birth or ritual, but how a person actually lives.
